title: Hybrid parser + FFI shared mempool investigation
content:
Summary:

This doc collects experiments and hypotheses from a week-long investigation into an intermittent CPU saturation pattern we see on medium payload traffic (avg tokens 80-200). Symptoms: sustained 60-85% CPU on frontend workers while GPU utilization is normal, tail latency spikes on small- and mid-sized batches, and large variance in tokenization + header-parse time across requests. The pattern is correlated with a recent hybrid parsing change that introduced a C++ FFI path for header/token scanning with a shared memory pool to avoid per-request allocations.

Goals:
- Understand whether the shared mempool FFI path is causing CPU-side contention or cache-thrashing.
- Quantify Python vs FFI time slices and identify blocking points (GIL, syscalls, locking).
- Propose low-risk mitigations (tweaked mempool sizing, per-thread pools, non-blocking handoff).

Observed behavior (high level):
- On 16-core nodes with 32 frontend workers, overall system CPU is high but distributed unevenly: some workers busy compiling/updating pools, others idle.
- py-spy sampling during spikes shows heavy stacks in parse_header_fn (C++) and in the Python wrapper that grabs the pool lock.
- perf flamegraphs show repeated wakeups at lock contended sites, and syscalls related to futex.
- Latency histograms show P95 for request-parse ballooning from ~6ms to ~45ms during incidents.

Repro recipe (local):
- Use the small-load generator (tests/loadgen/medium_payload.py) with concurrency=200, qps=500.
- Start local runtime with env DEBUG_PARSE_STATS=1 and MP_POOL_SIZE=1024.
- Capture profiles:
  - sudo perf record -F 99 -p <pid> -g -- sleep 60
  - py-spy record -o pyspy.svg --pid <pid> --duration 60 --native
  - python tools/small-flamegraph.py perf.data > perf.svg

Microbenchmarks run:
- Baseline: pure-Python header parse (no FFI) throughput ~ 27k req/s on 4 workers (median single-core).
- FFI + global mempool (current prod): throughput ~ 31k req/s at low concurrency but degrades to ~9k req/s under contended concurrency ramp.
- FFI + per-thread mempool (prototype): stable ~29k req/s across concurrency, significantly reduced futex/syscall counts.

Key measurements (representative):
- futex_wait/futex_wake rates (proc stat) climbed 4x during spike windows (baseline 120/s -> 480/s).
- scheduler migrations: increased context switches from 1.1k/s to 3.7k/s during incidents.
- percent time in C++ parse function: 36% (baseline 22%). Python wrapper lock acquisition accounted for ~14% CPU.

Hypotheses:
1) Global shared mempool introduces hot lock on allocation path; under concurrency this becomes the bottleneck and produces lock convoy effects (futex thrashing).
2) The Python->C++ FFI boundary is safe but our wrapper holds GIL while performing bookkeeping (pool index, stats), amplifying Python overhead under concurrency.
3) Cache-line ping-pong: the mempool head/tail pointers are touching adjacent slots used by other threads; false-sharing causes higher L1 eviction and increased cycles per op.

Experiments performed and results:
- Replace global mempool lock with per-thread slab allocation (no shared lock): contention drops dramatically, futex counts back to baseline, tail latency reduced by ~3x during peak QPS.
- Move bookkeeping out of GIL-protected region: unprotected C++ bookkeeping plus atomic stats increment lower Python time by ~9%. But this required careful refcounting; validated with ASAN and valgrind on a smaller run.
- Add padding to mempool control structure (align to cacheline): small but measurable reduction in cycles/instruction in microbench (6% improvement).
- Instrumented handoff: added a try-lock fast path with fallback to per-thread spill instead of blocking; reduced tail latencies but increased memory churn. Trade-off acceptable for Dedicated tier only.

Open items / unknowns:
- Multi-process deployment: current tests are single-process with many threads. In containers we run multiple worker processes; need to validate if per-thread mempool per-process scales when combined with multi-process layout.
- Memory footprint vs latency trade: per-thread mempools increase resident set size. Need to approximate additional memory at 1000 concurrent threads (estimate ~32MB per 256-slot pool).
- Edge cases with long-lived requests that hold a tokenization allocation across the network wait; this leaks mempool slots and may starve other requests. Consider time-based reclamation or epoch-based pooling.

Recommended mitigations (short-term):
- Roll out per-worker (process) mempool variant to edge fleet in canary (10% of traffic) for 48h to verify cross-process behavior. Config: MP_POOL_STRATEGY=per_shard, MP_POOL_SIZE=512, MP_PADDING=64.
- Remove bookkeeping from GIL path: require PR that moves stats to C++ atomics; add unit tests and ASAN.
- Add metrics: allocator_wait_time_ms, allocator_futex_count, allocator_spill_rate. Expose in console as per-route diagnostics.

Recommended mitigations (medium-term):
- Implement per-CPU freelist with fallback to global slab as last resort. This gives low-latency on hot paths and bounded memory.
- Rework API to return a lightweight token object that does not require Python refcounting on common path (reduce interactions with GIL).
- Add mempool leak watchdog that emits an alert if holder duration > 5s.

Proposed rollout plan:
1) Merge per-process mempool prototype behind feature flag. Smoke test with local loadgen and CI smoke.
2) Canary to 10% for 48h with debug metrics. Monitor allocator_wait_time_ms and P95 latency.
3) If stable, expand to 50% and enable padding and try-lock spill path.
4) Full rollout with metric-based auto-disable if allocator_wait_time_ms > 20ms for 5m.

Notes for engineering implementation:
- Keep pools allocated from posix_memalign to ensure alignment opportunity for metadata.
- Use C++ std::atomic for head/tail where possible; avoid locks in fast path.
- Avoid exposing raw pointers to Python; use small integer handles validated in C++ to prevent accidental ref leaks.
- Add deterministic unit tests that exercise pool refill and spill logic under fake concurrency (thread sanitizer + fake timers).

Next steps (action items):
- Ethan: open PR to surface allocator metrics and move stats out of GIL (due 2024-11-18).
- Mei: finish per-process mempool dogfood build and run 24h canary locally (due 2024-11-17).
- Liam: benchmark memory overhead across typical fleet instance types and produce cost estimate (due 2024-11-20).
- Priya: coordinate canary config and prepare dashboard panels (due 2024-11-16).

Appendix (traces & sample commands):
- py-spy: py-spy record -o /tmp/pyspy.svg --pid <pid> --native --duration 60
- perf: sudo perf record -F 200 -p <pid> -g -- sleep 60; sudo perf script | ./stackcollapse-perf.pl > out.folded; ./flamegraph.pl out.folded > perf.svg
- counters: for i in $(seq 1 10); do cat /proc/<pid>/stack | wc -l; sleep 1; done
- small microbench: tests/bench/mempool_micro.py --threads 32 --ops 100000 --pool-size 512

Raw experiment notes (short):
- 2024-11-04: initial reproducer; confirmed futex storm; created JIRA SRV-987.
- 2024-11-06: per-thread mempool POC; observed big wins on synthetic.
- 2024-11-11: padding + try-lock reduced syscalls but increased RSS by ~12MB per worker.
- 2024-11-14: validated atomic bookkeeping approach under ASAN; ready for PR.

If you were debugging this from scratch, start with the perf + py-spy combo and then verify futex counts and syscall patterns. Focus on lock hotspots and GIL-holding code in the wrapper. The simplest fast win is to avoid taking a shared lock on the hot allocation path; the per-thread/per-process pool variant is low-risk and observable with the added metrics.

End of doc.
